'''''Erythrina variegata''''', commonly known as '''tiger's claw'''<ref name=EPPO>{{cite web | title = ''Erythrina variegata'' | url = https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/ERZVA | publisher = [[European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization]] (EPPO) | access-date = 26 August 2021}}</ref> or '''Indian coral tree''',<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | access-date = 18 December 2017}}</ref> is a species of ''[[Erythrina]]'' native to the tropical and subtropical regions of eastern Africa, the [[Indian subcontinent]], northern Australia, and the islands of the Indian Ocean and the western Pacific Ocean east to [[Fiji]].<ref name=grin/>

==Description==

[[File:Flower I IMG 3974.jpg|thumb|right|Flower in [[Kolkata]], India]]
''E. variegata'' is a thorny [[deciduous]] [[tree]] growing to {{convert|27|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall. The [[leaf|leaves]] are pinnate with a {{convert|20|cm|abbr=on}} [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] and three leaflets, each leaflet up to {{convert|20|cm|abbr=on}} long and broad. It has dense clusters of scarlet or crimson [[flower]]s and black [[seed]]s.<ref name=rhs>{{cite book | editor = Huxley, A. | date = 1992 | title = New RHS Dictionary of Gardening | publisher = Macmillan | isbn = 0-333-47494-5}}</ref>

Notably, crows have been observed contributing to the pollination of the Indian coral tree by feeding on its nectar-rich flowers.{{citation needed|date=May 2024}}

== Uses ==

''Erythrina variegata'' is valued as an [[ornamental tree]]. Several [[cultivar]]s have been selected, including 'Alba' with white flowers.<ref name=rhs/>

In Vietnam, the leaves are used to wrap [[nem chua|fermented meat]] ({{langx|vi|nem}}).

''E. variegata'' is known as '''''dapdap''''' in many languages of the [[Philippines]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://acd.clld.org/cognatesets/30231#2/1.5/138.3|title= *''dapdap''₁ a tree with dense clusters of red flowers, the Indian coral tree, Erythrina indica |last1=Blust|first1=Robert|last2=Trussel|first2=Stephen|website=Austronesian Comparative Dictionary|date=2010|publisher=Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology|access-date=10 November 2022}}</ref> where its bark and leaves are used in alternative medicine.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.stuartxchange.org/Dapdap.html|title=Dapdap / Erythrina variegata / Indian coral tree: Philippine Medicinal Herbs / Philippine Alternative Medicine|website=www.stuartxchange.org|access-date=2017-03-10}}</ref>

''E. variegata'' is often used in agroforestry systems. It can be used for fodder as its foliage has a good nutritive value for most livestock.<ref>Heuzé V., Thiollet H., Tran G., Edouard N., Lebas F., 2018. Coral tree (Erythrina variegata). Feedipedia, a programme by INRA, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO. https://www.feedipedia.org/node/23080</ref>

The seeds are poisonous in their raw state but can be cooked and eaten. Along with the bark, the seeds were used to stupefy fish, making them easier to catch.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hargreaves|first1=Dorothy|last2=Hargreaves|first2=Bob|title=Tropical Trees of the Pacific|year=1970|publisher=Hargreaves|location=Kailua, Hawaii|page=24}}</ref>

The Formosan aboriginal [[Puyuma people|Puyuma]] tribe carve a [[Mortar and pestle|mortar]] called a taur from the trunk of the tree. It is used for pounding sticky rice that is later to be steamed.{{citation needed|date=April 2020}}

==Cultural impact==
''E. variegata'' was designated the official flower of [[Okinawa Prefecture]] in 1967. The ''deigo'' flower features in the popular song "[[Shima Uta (The Boom)|Shima Uta]]" by [[The Boom]], one of the most well-known songs associated with Okinawa. In addition, the use of the wood of the ''deigo'' tree is one of the unique characteristics of [[Ryukyuan lacquerware]].

In Sri Lanka, the blossoming flowers of the tree are associated with the advent of the Sri Lankan (April) New Year. This plant is known as ''Erabadu'' ([[Sinhala language|Sinhala]]: එරබදු) in Sinhalese.

In [[Fiji]] —known as ''drala'', ''drara'' or ''rara''— its flowering season marks the traditional time to plant [[taro]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Keppel |first1=Gunnar |title=Trees of Fiji: A Guide to 100 Rainforest Trees |last2=Ghazanfar |first2=Shahina A. |author-link2=Shahina A. Ghazanfar |date=2011 |publisher=Secretariat of the Pacific Community & Deutsche Gesellschaft für Technische Zusammenarbeit |edition=third, revised |pages=156–7}}</ref> In [[Mangaia]], it marks the arrival of [[Kingfisher|kingfishers]] and the nesting of [[black-winged petrel]]s.<ref>{{cite web |title=Erythrina variegata - Coral Tree |url=http://data.bishopmuseum.org/pbs/cookislands/species.asp?id=6119 |access-date=3 January 2023 |website=Cook Islands Biodiversity |publisher=[[Bishop Museum]] |archive-date=3 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230103013112/http://data.bishopmuseum.org/pbs/cookislands/species.asp?id=6119 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Role in ecosystem==
[[Fiji crested iguana]]s can be found within ''Erythrina variegata'' ("''rara''") trees.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Harlow|first1=Peter S.|display-authors=etal|year=2009|title=Critically Endangered Fijian Crested Iguana (''Brachylophus vitiensis'') Shows Habitat Preference For Globally Threatened Tropical Dry Forest|journal=Pacific Science|volume=63|issue=2|pages=223–242|doi=10.2984/049.063.0205|hdl=20.500.11937/14711|s2cid=53469707 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>{{rp|229, 240}}
